title: Certified Kubernetes Administrator
tagline: CKA: clusters, workloads, storage, networking, troubleshooting
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the CNCF or the Linux Foundation. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: Which component does what?
scenarios.situation: A new hire asks why the cluster needs so many binaries: kube-apiserver, etcd, kube-scheduler, kube-controller-manager on the control plane, plus kubelet and kube-proxy on every node.
scenarios.prompt: Match each control-plane component to its job.
choices: apiserver: the API front door; etcd: the cluster's state store; scheduler: assigns Pods to nodes; controller-manager: runs reconciliation loops
apiserver: stores state; etcd: schedules Pods; scheduler: exposes the API; controller-manager: runs containers
All four are redundant copies of the same API server for HA
apiserver and etcd run on workers; scheduler and controller-manager run on control plane nodes only
scenarios.why: The apiserver is the only component clients talk to; etcd is the consistent key-value store of record; the scheduler binds unscheduled Pods to nodes; the controller-manager runs controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node) that reconcile desired vs actual state. kubelet (node agent) and kube-proxy (service networking) run on every node including control-plane nodes.
scenarios.hint: Which component is the single source of truth for cluster state?

scenarios.title: Back up etcd before the upgrade
scenarios.situation: Before upgrading the cluster you must snapshot etcd. You run 'etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db' and get an error about the API version and connection refused.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct snapshot command shape on a kubeadm cluster?
choices: ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=<ca> --cert=<cert> --key=<key> snapshot save /backup/etcd.db
etcdctl backup --data-dir /var/lib/etcd /backup/etcd.db
kubectl backup etcd --all-namespaces -o /backup/etcd.db
cp /var/lib/etcd/member/snap/db /backup/etcd.db while etcd is running
scenarios.why: Modern etcd needs ETCDCTL_API=3, the TLS endpoint, and the cluster's client certificates (found in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/). 'snapshot save' is the online backup API; copying the data dir of a running etcd risks corruption, and there is no 'kubectl backup etcd'.
scenarios.hint: Does etcd's API listen on plaintext localhost by default in kubeadm?

scenarios.title: Upgrade order matters
scenarios.situation: Your cluster runs v1.30 everywhere. You want v1.33. A teammate suggests upgrading kubelets first since they're 'just agents'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the supported upgrade order and version-skew rule?
choices: Upgrade control plane first (kubeadm upgrade apply), then kubelets — kubelet must never be newer than the apiserver and may lag by up to two minor versions
Upgrade kubelets first — agents are stateless and version-independent
Upgrade everything simultaneously with a single command
Version skew doesn't matter as long as kubectl matches the server
scenarios.why: The supported skew policy: kube-apiserver first, then controller-manager/scheduler, then kubelets. kubelet can be at most two minor versions older than the apiserver (n-2) and never newer; kubectl must be within one minor version of the apiserver. kubeadm enforces this via 'kubeadm upgrade plan'.
scenarios.hint: Which component must always be the newest in the cluster?

scenarios.title: The apiserver that starts itself
scenarios.situation: After a control-plane node reboot, kube-apiserver is running even though no Deployment or systemd unit for it exists. You find a YAML file under /etc/kubernetes/manifests/.
scenarios.prompt: What is this, and how is it managed?
choices: A static Pod — the kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests and runs any Pod YAML placed there, mirroring it to the apiserver
A systemd service disguised as YAML — kubelet ignores that directory
A CronJob that restarts the apiserver on boot
An init container left over from kubeadm init
scenarios.why: kubeadm deploys control-plane components as static Pods: plain Pod manifests in the kubelet's manifest directory (--pod-manifest-path, default /etc/kubernetes/manifests). The kubelet starts them without any apiserver involvement — which is exactly why the apiserver itself can be deployed this way. Edit the file and the kubelet restarts the Pod.
scenarios.hint: What reads that directory — the apiserver, or something that runs before it?

scenarios.title: Adding a worker securely
scenarios.situation: You run 'kubeadm init' on the first control-plane node. Now you need to join two workers. The join command from init output has expired.
scenarios.prompt: How do you generate a fresh, secure join command?
choices: On the control plane: 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' — it issues a new bootstrap token and prints the full join with CA hash
Copy /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf to the workers — that's sufficient for joining
Reuse any old token — bootstrap tokens never expire
Run 'kubeadm init' on each worker too
scenarios.why: kubeadm join needs a bootstrap token (default TTL 24h) plus the CA cert hash for trust. 'kubeadm token create --print-join-command' mints a fresh token and prints the complete, verified command. admin.conf grants cluster-admin — copying it to workers is a security anti-pattern, and running init twice creates two clusters.
scenarios.hint: What two secrets does a joining node need to trust and authenticate to the cluster?

scenarios.title: Pods can't resolve service names
scenarios.situation: Pods run fine and can ping each other by IP, but 'nslookup api.default' fails inside Pods. The cluster was just rebuilt with a new CNI.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you look first?
choices: Check CoreDNS Pods and the kube-dns Service — pod DNS depends on CoreDNS, independent of the CNI
Reinstall the CNI — name resolution is a CNI responsibility
Check kube-proxy — it provides DNS for Services
Restart all Pods — DNS config is cached permanently at Pod creation
scenarios.why: In-cluster DNS is served by CoreDNS (fronted by the kube-dns Service at 10.96.0.10 by default); the CNI only provides pod networking. /etc/resolv.conf in each Pod points at kube-dns. If CoreDNS Pods are CrashLooping or the Service selector is broken, name resolution fails while IP connectivity works.
scenarios.hint: Which cluster component answers DNS queries from Pods?

scenarios.title: Keep non-GPU work off GPU nodes
scenarios.situation: You add 2 expensive GPU nodes. Regular Pods keep landing on them, wasting money. You want ONLY GPU workloads to schedule there.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct taint + toleration design?
choices: Taint the GPU nodes with dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule; add a matching toleration ONLY to GPU workload Pods
Taint the GPU nodes and add the toleration to every Pod so nothing breaks
Use nodeSelector on the regular Pods to avoid GPU nodes
Taints can't do this — you need a separate cluster
scenarios.why: Taints repel Pods that don't tolerate them: 'kubectl taint nodes gpu1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule'. Only Pods with the matching toleration (key dedicated, value gpu, effect NoSchedule) schedule there. NoSchedule blocks new scheduling; NoExecute would also evict running Pods. nodeSelector on regular Pods doesn't scale — taint the special nodes instead.
scenarios.hint: Do you label the special nodes, or label everything else?

scenarios.title: SSD-only database
scenarios.situation: Your database needs nodes with SSDs, labeled disktype=ssd. As a soft preference you'd also like zone-a, but the DB must run even if zone-a is full.
scenarios.prompt: How do you express a hard SSD requirement plus a soft zone preference?
choices: nodeAffinity: requiredDuringScheduling for disktype=ssd, plus preferredDuringScheduling with a weight for zone-a
nodeSelector for both — preferences aren't supported
Two separate Deployments — one per zone
Taint all non-SSD nodes with NoExecute
scenarios.why: Node affinity splits hard vs soft: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is mandatory (Pod stays pending without SSD nodes); preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution adds weighted scoring the scheduler tries to satisfy. nodeSelector only does hard equality matching. 'IgnoredDuringExecution' means the rule isn't re-evaluated if labels change later.
scenarios.hint: Which affinity stanza is mandatory and which is best-effort?

scenarios.title: Don't put all replicas together
scenarios.situation: Your 3-replica API keeps landing all Pods on the same node — one node failure takes the whole API down.
scenarios.prompt: What spreads them across nodes?
choices: podAntiAffinity with requiredDuringScheduling on hostname topology, matching the API's own labels
podAffinity — it spreads Pods apart
Increase replicas to 10 — spreading happens automatically
Taint the node after scheduling — Pods will redistribute
scenarios.why: podAntiAffinity repels: 'don't schedule me on a node (topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname) already running a Pod matching these labels'. requiredDuringScheduling makes it a hard rule. podAffinity does the opposite (co-locate). Replica count alone never guarantees spread — that's also what topologySpreadConstraints handle more flexibly.
scenarios.hint: Affinity attracts, anti-affinity repels — which do you need?

scenarios.title: Which Pod gets killed first?
scenarios.situation: A node runs out of memory. Three Pods: A (requests=limits set for all containers), B (requests set, no limits), C (no requests or limits). The kubelet must evict.
scenarios.prompt: What are their QoS classes and eviction order?
choices: A=Guaranteed, B=Burstable, C=BestEffort — BestEffort dies first, then Burstable, Guaranteed last
All three are BestEffort — classes only apply to CPU
A=Burstable, B=Guaranteed, C=BestEffort — Guaranteed dies first
QoS classes are just labels — eviction is random
scenarios.why: QoS is derived: Guaranteed = requests == limits for every container (CPU and memory); Burstable = at least one request/limit set but not equal; BestEffort = nothing set. Under memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable (by how far over requests), protecting Guaranteed longest. Always set requests AND limits on critical workloads.
scenarios.hint: Which Pod made no resource promises at all?

scenarios.title: Log collector on every node
scenarios.situation: You need a log-shipping agent on every node, including nodes added next month. A Deployment with 5 replicas won't cover future nodes.
scenarios.prompt: Which workload type fits, and why not a Deployment?
choices: DaemonSet — it ensures one Pod per (matching) node automatically, including future nodes
StatefulSet — it's designed for per-node agents
A static Pod copied to every node manually
A Job with parallelism equal to node count
scenarios.why: DaemonSet's contract is 'one Pod per selected node': the controller adds Pods as nodes join and removes them as nodes leave — perfect for node-level agents (log shippers, monitoring, CNI). Deployments manage a fixed replica count with no node awareness; StatefulSets give stable identity/storage, not per-node coverage.
scenarios.hint: Which controller reacts to nodes joining the cluster?

scenarios.title: Draining for maintenance
scenarios.situation: You must reboot node worker-3 for kernel patching. Running 'kubectl delete node' would be wrong, and just rebooting would kill Pods ungracefully.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct sequence?
choices: kubectl cordon worker-3, then kubectl drain worker-3 --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data; reboot; kubectl uncordon worker-3
kubectl drain worker-3 --force without cordon — drain implies cordon
Delete all Pods on the node manually, then reboot
kubectl taint worker-3 maintenance=true:NoSchedule — that's sufficient
scenarios.why: cordon marks the node unschedulable; drain evicts Pods gracefully (respecting PodDisruptionBudgets) and cordons as part of the operation — though explicit cordon first is the safe habit. --ignore-daemonsets skips DaemonSet Pods (they can't be drained), --delete-emptydir-data acknowledges local data loss. uncordon returns the node to service after the reboot.
scenarios.hint: What two things must happen: stop new Pods arriving, and move existing ones away safely?

scenarios.title: The full DNS name
scenarios.situation: A Pod in namespace 'frontend' needs to reach the 'api' Service in namespace 'backend'. 'http://api' doesn't resolve.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct fully-qualified name, and why did the short name fail?
choices: api.backend.svc.cluster.local — short names only resolve within the same namespace (via the Pod's search domains)
api.backend — the svc and cluster.local suffixes are optional
http://api:backend — namespaces are ports
Services can't be reached across namespaces — duplicate the Service
scenarios.why: Cluster DNS form: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. A Pod's resolv.conf search domains include '<pod-namespace>.svc.cluster.local', so short 'api' expands within its own namespace only. Cross-namespace requires at least 'api.backend' (resolvable via search) — the FQDN always works.
scenarios.hint: What search domains does a Pod get, and which namespace do they cover?

scenarios.title: HTTPS for the app
scenarios.situation: You have an Ingress routing / to the web Service. Now you need HTTPS with certificate 'web-tls' for host app.example.com.
scenarios.prompt: What does the Ingress need?
choices: A tls: section listing hosts: [app.example.com] and secretName: web-tls (a kubernetes.io/tls Secret), plus an IngressClass
TLS is automatic — Ingresses serve HTTPS by default
Add the certificate as an annotation string on the Service
Ingress can't do TLS — use a LoadBalancer Service instead
scenarios.why: Ingress TLS: spec.tls[] maps hosts to a TLS Secret (type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt/tls.key). The ingress controller (nginx, etc., selected via ingressClassName) terminates TLS. Without the tls section you get HTTP only. cert-manager automates issuance/renewal via ACME.
scenarios.hint: Where does the certificate live, and how does the Ingress reference it?

scenarios.title: Allow only the API to reach the DB
scenarios.situation: Namespace 'data' runs Postgres. Only Pods labeled app=api in namespace 'backend' may connect to port 5432. Everything else is denied.
scenarios.prompt: What does the NetworkPolicy look like?
choices: podSelector matching postgres, policyTypes: [Ingress], ingress from: podSelector app=api + namespaceSelector for backend, ports: [5432]
An egress policy on the backend namespace — ingress policies can't filter by namespace
A Service of type LoadBalancer with a firewall annotation
NetworkPolicies can't express cross-namespace rules
scenarios.why: NetworkPolicy ingress.from combines podSelector (who) with namespaceSelector (where) — both in one peer entry means AND. policyTypes: Ingress activates ingress enforcement; the podSelector selects the DB Pods; ports restrict to 5432. Remember: the policy must exist in the DB's namespace, and the CNI must enforce policies.
scenarios.hint: In which namespace does the policy live, and what does 'from' combine?

scenarios.title: NodePort rejected
scenarios.situation: You create a NodePort Service requesting port 8080. The API server rejects it as out of range.
scenarios.prompt: Why, and what are the options?
choices: Default NodePort range is 30000–32767 — pick a port in range or omit nodePort to auto-assign
NodePorts must be below 1024 — use 80
The port is in use — NodePorts can't be specified at all
Services can't expose ports — use hostNetwork instead
scenarios.why: The apiserver's --service-node-port-range defaults to 30000-32767; explicitly requested nodePorts outside it are rejected. Omit nodePort for auto-allocation, or choose within range. (The range is configurable cluster-wide, but you won't change it per-Service.) For production external access, prefer Ingress/LoadBalancer over NodePort.
scenarios.hint: What is the default valid range for nodePort values?

scenarios.title: Debugging DNS from inside
scenarios.situation: Pods can't resolve 'db.data'. You need to test DNS from inside the cluster, inspect resolv.conf, and query the cluster DNS directly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the standard debug approach?
choices: Run a temporary debug Pod (e.g., kubectl run -it dns-test --image=busybox --restart=Never), then nslookup/db.data and cat /etc/resolv.conf inside it
nslookup from your laptop — it uses the same DNS
Restart CoreDNS — debugging is unnecessary
Edit /etc/resolv.conf on the nodes — Pods inherit it directly
scenarios.why: Debug from inside the cluster's network: a throwaway Pod with dnsutils/busybox lets you run nslookup <name>, check /etc/resolv.conf (nameserver should be the kube-dns ClusterIP, searches set), and query specific servers ('nslookup db.data 10.96.0.10'). Your laptop's DNS is irrelevant. 'kubectl debug' adds ephemeral containers to existing Pods for the same purpose.
scenarios.hint: Where must the test run to see what Pods see?

scenarios.title: How Services get their VIP
scenarios.situation: A junior asks how a ClusterIP (a fake IP nothing is bound to) actually delivers packets to Pods.
scenarios.prompt: What does kube-proxy do, and what are its modes?
choices: kube-proxy programs packet routing on each node — iptables mode writes NAT rules, IPVS mode uses kernel IPVS for larger scale
kube-proxy is a userspace proxy that terminates every connection
The apiserver routes Service traffic directly
ClusterIPs are real interfaces created on each node
scenarios.why: kube-proxy watches Services/Endpoints and programs the data path on every node: iptables mode installs NAT rules (simple, scales to ~thousands of services), IPVS mode uses Linux IPVS (better load-balancing algorithms, scales further). The old userspace mode is obsolete. The ClusterIP exists only as routing rules — nothing listens on it.
scenarios.hint: Which component translates the virtual Service IP into Pod IPs on each node?

scenarios.title: The PVC that won't bind
scenarios.situation: You create a PVC requesting 10Gi ReadWriteOnce. It sits in Pending. A 5Gi PV exists, plus a StorageClass with dynamic provisioning.
scenarios.prompt: Why is it Pending, and what are the possible fixes?
choices: No suitable PV: the 5Gi PV is too small and (if no default StorageClass or provisioner can't satisfy it) nothing dynamically provisions — create a matching PV or fix the StorageClass
PVCs bind to any PV regardless of size — this is a bug
Pending means bound — the app can use it
Delete the PV — PVCs create their own storage
scenarios.why: Binding requires: sufficient capacity, compatible accessModes, matching storageClassName (or both empty), and selector/label match. A 5Gi PV can't satisfy 10Gi. With a default StorageClass, dynamic provisioning should create a volume — if it doesn't, check the provisioner, parameters, and events ('kubectl describe pvc'). Fix: right-size a static PV or repair dynamic provisioning.
scenarios.hint: What must match between a PV and a PVC for binding?

scenarios.title: Sharing storage between Pods
scenarios.situation: Two Pods on different nodes need read-write access to the same dataset. You provision ReadWriteOnce storage and the second Pod can't mount it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the access-mode issue, and what are the options?
choices: ReadWriteOnce = one node at a time — you need ReadWriteMany (shared filesystems like NFS/EFS) or an object store / replicated DB instead of shared POSIX
Access modes are advisory — force-mount it on both
RWO means one Pod total — delete the first Pod
All storage is ReadWriteMany by default — the provisioner is broken
scenarios.why: Access modes: RWO (one node RW), ROX (many nodes read-only), RWX (many nodes RW). Most block storage (EBS, GCE PD) is RWO-only — the second node's mount fails by design. True shared RW needs a shared filesystem (NFS, EFS, CephFS, Azure Files). Often the better architecture is avoiding shared POSIX: object storage or a database.
scenarios.hint: What does 'Once' vs 'Many' count — Pods or nodes?

scenarios.title: The missing default
scenarios.situation: PVCs without storageClassName stay Pending, though a StorageClass 'fast' exists. On another cluster, identical PVCs bind immediately.
scenarios.prompt: What differs between the clusters?
choices: The working cluster marks a StorageClass as default (annotation storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class=true) — without it, PVCs with no class only bind pre-provisioned matching PVs
StorageClasses are cluster-global — defaults don't exist
PVCs always need explicit storageClassName — the other cluster is misbehaving
Dynamic provisioning works without any StorageClass
scenarios.why: A PVC with no storageClassName binds only to PVs with no class — unless a default StorageClass exists, in which case it's applied automatically and dynamic provisioning kicks in. One default per cluster (the annotation). 'kubectl get storageclass' shows it. This is the #1 'works in dev, Pending in prod' storage gotcha.
scenarios.hint: What annotation makes a StorageClass apply to class-less PVCs?

scenarios.title: Growing a live volume
scenarios.situation: A 20Gi database volume is 95% full. Downtime for a restore is unacceptable. The StorageClass has allowVolumeExpansion: true.
scenarios.prompt: What is the expansion procedure?
choices: Edit the PVC to 40Gi (kubectl edit pvc) — the provisioner expands the volume; then expand the filesystem (often automatic; else resize2fs/xfs_growfs via the Pod)
Delete the PVC and recreate it bigger — data is preserved
Volumes can't be expanded — restore from backup to a bigger one
Edit the PV directly — PVCs are immutable in size
scenarios.why: With allowVolumeExpansion: true and a supporting provisioner/driver, PVCs are editable upward: the external-resizer expands the block device, and kubelet expands the filesystem (FileSystemResizePending → done, often automatic for mounted volumes). Only expansion, never shrinking. Verify with 'kubectl get pvc' and df inside the Pod.
scenarios.hint: Which StorageClass field gates whether PVCs can grow?

scenarios.title: Stable storage per replica
scenarios.situation: A 3-replica database needs each replica to keep its own data across reschedules — replica-0 must always get replica-0's data back.
scenarios.prompt: Which workload + storage pattern gives stable per-replica storage?
choices: StatefulSet with volumeClaimTemplates — each Pod gets a stable-named PVC (data-db-0) that follows the Pod's identity
Deployment with one shared PVC — replicas coordinate writes
DaemonSet with hostPath — simplest stable storage
emptyDir — it's per-Pod already
scenarios.why: StatefulSets give stable identity: Pod db-0 ↔ PVC data-db-0 via volumeClaimTemplates (auto-created per replica). On reschedule, db-0 reattaches to its own PVC. Deployments have interchangeable Pods with no identity — wrong for stateful data. hostPath ties data to a node (lost on reschedule); emptyDir dies with the Pod.
scenarios.hint: Which workload gives each replica a stable name — and what storage follows that name?

scenarios.title: The data survived the PVC
scenarios.situation: You delete a PVC. The PV goes to 'Released' and the underlying cloud disk still exists — and still bills you. You expected automatic cleanup.
scenarios.prompt: What controls this, and what are the policies?
choices: The PV's persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain (keep the volume, manual cleanup) vs Delete (remove the volume when the PVC is deleted)
Reclaim policies don't exist — deletion always cleans up
The StorageClass controls it — PVs have no policy
Released means deleted — the billing is a cloud bug
scenarios.why: Reclaim policy is per-PV (defaulting from the StorageClass): Retain keeps the underlying volume after PVC deletion (data safe, manual cleanup, PV goes Released and can't rebind without manual intervention); Delete removes the volume asset. Dynamically provisioned volumes usually default Delete; statically created PVs default Retain. Check before deleting PVCs holding important data.
scenarios.hint: Which policy keeps the cloud disk after the PVC is gone?

scenarios.title: CrashLoopBackOff
scenarios.situation: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. 'kubectl logs' shows nothing useful — the container dies too fast. Describe shows the container restarting every few seconds.
scenarios.prompt: What is your systematic debug sequence?
choices: kubectl logs --previous (last crashed instance), check the command/args and env in the spec, verify probes aren't killing a slow starter, then kubectl exec/debug if it stays up briefly
Delete the Pod — CrashLoopBackOff resolves itself
Scale to 0 and back — that fixes the image
Restart kubelet on the node — it's a node problem
scenarios.why: CrashLoopBackOff = container exits, kubelet backs off restarts. Debug: --previous for the dead container's logs; common causes — bad command/args, missing env/config, failing startupProbe/livenessProbe killing slow boots, immediate exit (no foreground process). 'kubectl debug' adds an ephemeral container to a running Pod for inspection without changing the image.
scenarios.hint: Where are the logs of the container instance that already died?

scenarios.title: ImagePullBackOff
scenarios.situation: A new Deployment's Pods are ImagePullBackOff. Events say 'unauthorized: authentication required'. The image is in a private registry.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing, and how do you attach it?
choices: An imagePullSecret — create a docker-registry Secret and reference it in the Pod spec's imagePullSecrets (or attach to the ServiceAccount)
The image doesn't exist — private registries can't be used
Pull the image manually on each node with docker pull
ImagePullBackOff means the tag is wrong — only the tag matters
scenarios.why: kubelet needs registry credentials: 'kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...', then imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}] in the Pod spec (or on the ServiceAccount for all its Pods). Also check: typo'd image/tag, and whether the registry requires the full path. Describe the Pod — events name the exact failure.
scenarios.hint: How does the kubelet authenticate to a private registry?

scenarios.title: Pod stuck Pending
scenarios.situation: A Pod with a PVC and 8Gi memory request sits Pending. Events: '0/3 nodes are available: 3 Insufficient memory, 1 persistentvolumeclaim not found'.
scenarios.prompt: How do you read and resolve this?
choices: Two independent problems: the PVC doesn't exist (create/fix it) and no node has 8Gi free (lower the request or add capacity) — events list all unsatisfied predicates
Pending is normal — wait 24 hours
Delete the scheduler Pod — it's stuck
Pending means the image is pulling — just slow
scenarios.why: 'kubectl describe pod' Events show each failed scheduling predicate. Here: unbound PVC (no matching PV/StorageClass provisioning) AND insufficient memory. Fix each: provision storage / correct the claim; right-size requests or scale the cluster. Pending is the scheduler telling you exactly what's wrong — read the events.
scenarios.hint: How many distinct reasons does the event list?

scenarios.title: Node NotReady
scenarios.situation: 'kubectl get nodes' shows worker-2 NotReady. Pods on it are being evicted. You have SSH access.
scenarios.prompt: What is your triage order?
choices: kubectl describe node (conditions: DiskPressure/MemoryPressure/NetworkUnavailable), then on-node: kubelet status/logs, disk space, container runtime health
Delete the node object — Kubernetes recreates it
Reboot immediately — diagnosis wastes time
NotReady is cosmetic — workloads are fine
scenarios.why: Triage: describe node conditions (MemoryPressure/DiskPressure/PIDPressure explain evictions; NetworkUnavailable implicates CNI). Then node-level: 'systemctl status kubelet', 'journalctl -u kubelet', disk full? ('df -h'), runtime down? ('systemctl status containerd'). Fix the cause (free disk, restart runtime), the node returns Ready and Pods reschedule. Deleting the Node object orphans workloads.
scenarios.hint: What do the node's Conditions tell you before you SSH?

scenarios.title: Service unreachable by name
scenarios.situation: Pod A can't reach 'http://api:8080' but curls the ClusterIP directly fine. DNS is suspect.
scenarios.prompt: How do you isolate DNS vs networking?
choices: From a debug Pod: nslookup api (tests DNS), cat /etc/resolv.conf (nameserver should be kube-dns), nslookup api 10.96.0.10 (bypass search domains); check CoreDNS Pods
Restart all Pods — DNS caches permanently
It's always the CNI — reinstall it
Services don't get DNS — use IPs
scenarios.why: Direct-IP works + name fails = DNS problem (not CNI). Check: Pod's resolv.conf points at kube-dns Service IP; 'nslookup api' vs FQDN (search-domain issues); query kube-dns IP directly; CoreDNS Pods Running with clean logs; the 'api' Service actually has Endpoints. Layer the tests — each narrows the fault domain.
scenarios.hint: If the IP works but the name doesn't, which layer is broken?

scenarios.title: API server won't start
scenarios.situation: After a control-plane reboot, kubectl fails: 'connection refused' on 6443. kube-apiserver's static Pod keeps crashing.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you look, given the apiserver is down?
choices: kubelet logs + static Pod manifests (/etc/kubernetes/manifests): check apiserver's --etcd-servers and cert paths; verify etcd static Pod is healthy (etcd must be up first)
kubectl describe — it works without the apiserver
Reinstall the cluster — apiserver crashes are fatal
Wait — static Pods self-heal without etcd
scenarios.why: With the apiserver down, kubectl is useless — go to the node: 'journalctl -u kubelet', 'crictl ps/logs' for the static Pod containers, and the manifest YAMLs. The apiserver depends on etcd: if the etcd static Pod is crashlooping (disk full? cert expired? data corruption?), fix etcd first — the apiserver can't start without its state store. Check cert expiry with openssl on the pki files.
scenarios.hint: What does the apiserver need before it can serve anything?

scenarios.title: Can I do that?
scenarios.situation: A developer's deploy fails with 'forbidden: User cannot create deployments in namespace staging'. You need to check their effective permissions without asking them to try things.
scenarios.prompt: How do you audit what a subject can do?
choices: kubectl auth can-i create deployments --namespace staging --as=dev-user (and --list for the full set) — impersonation-based permission check
kubectl get roles — that shows effective permissions
Ask them to try again — errors are the audit
Check /etc/kubernetes/auth — the permission database
scenarios.why: 'kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns>' evaluates RBAC as that subject — the definitive 'can they?' check. '--list' dumps the full effective permission set. Remember RBAC is additive (union of all bindings); a single deny doesn't exist — least privilege means granting only what's needed.
scenarios.hint: Which command evaluates RBAC from another subject's perspective?

scenarios.title: The overexposed ServiceAccount
scenarios.situation: Every Pod in the cluster mounts the default ServiceAccount token, including a third-party metrics exporter that was just compromised. The token can list Pods cluster-wide (bound to a broad ClusterRole).
scenarios.prompt: What are the hardening steps?
choices: Scope the ClusterRoleBinding down to a RoleBinding (or least-privilege Role), set automountServiceAccountToken: false where unneeded, and use dedicated ServiceAccounts per workload
Delete all ServiceAccounts — Pods don't need them
Tokens are harmless — the compromise doesn't matter
Rotate the cluster CA — that invalidates tokens
scenarios.why: Hardening: per-workload ServiceAccounts (never share default), least-privilege Roles/RoleBindings, automountServiceAccountToken: false on Pods that don't call the API, and short-lived projected tokens (the default since 1.22 — auto-rotating, audience-bound). The default SA historically got overly broad bindings — audit yours.
scenarios.hint: Which Pods actually need to talk to the API server?

scenarios.title: Enforcing restricted cluster-wide
scenarios.situation: Security requires the 'restricted' Pod Security Standard enforced (not just warned) on all app namespaces, excluding kube-system.
scenarios.prompt: How do you implement this natively?
choices: Label each app namespace pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted (optionally with version pin); audit existing workloads with warn/audit modes first
Edit the apiserver flags — labels don't enforce
PodSecurityPolicy with restricted profile
RBAC can enforce Pod security fields directly
scenarios.why: The PodSecurity admission plugin reads namespace labels: enforce (blocks violations), audit (records), warn (warns) — each with a version (e.g., restricted:latest). Rollout strategy: warn/audit first to find violating workloads, fix them, then enforce. Exemptions for system namespaces via the plugin's exemptions config. PSP was removed in 1.25 — don't reach for it.
scenarios.hint: What namespace labels does the PodSecurity admission plugin read?

scenarios.title: Who deleted the namespace?
scenarios.situation: The 'payments' namespace vanished overnight. You need to know who did it and from where.
scenarios.prompt: What provides this forensic trail?
choices: The Kubernetes audit log (apiserver --audit-log-path with an audit policy) — records who did what, when, from where, with what result
kubectl get events — events persist indefinitely
The scheduler log — it records deletions
Audit logs don't exist in Kubernetes — check the cloud trail only
scenarios.why: Enable apiserver auditing: an audit policy selects which requests to log (e.g., all writes at RequestResponse level for sensitive resources), written as JSON to --audit-log-path (usually shipped to a SIEM). It captures user, source IP, verb, object, and response. Events are short-lived hints, not forensics — auditing is the compliance-grade trail.
scenarios.hint: Which apiserver log records every mutating request with user and source IP?

scenarios.title: Secrets in etcd, plaintext
scenarios.situation: Someone with etcd access dumped a Secret's value directly from the key-value store — base64'd but effectively plaintext.
scenarios.prompt: How do you encrypt Secrets at rest in etcd?
choices: EncryptionConfiguration with an AES-CBC (or secretbox/KMS) provider for the secrets resource — applied via --encryption-provider-config, then rewrite existing Secrets to re-encrypt
Secrets are encrypted by default — the dump must have been decrypted
RBAC prevents etcd access — no action needed
Encrypt each Secret's values manually before creating
scenarios.why: Enable envelope encryption: EncryptionConfiguration listing providers (aescbc with local keys, or KMS plugins) for resource 'secrets', passed to kube-apiserver. Crucially, existing Secrets must be re-encrypted ('kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -') — the config only encrypts new writes. Rotate keys via the key-rotation procedure; back up the config — losing keys loses Secrets.
scenarios.hint: What must happen to Secrets written BEFORE encryption was enabled?

scenarios.title: Locking down the Pod spec
scenarios.situation: Your app Pods run as root, allow privilege escalation, and mount the root filesystem writable. Security wants all three fixed in the Pod spec.
scenarios.prompt: Which securityContext fields address each?
choices: runAsNonRoot: true (+ runAsUser), allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true — plus capabilities drop: [ALL]
privileged: false — the single field covers everything
These can't be set in the spec — only via admission
Run as root but add a NetworkPolicy — equivalent protection
scenarios.why: Pod/container securityContext hardening: runAsNonRoot/runAsUser (no root), allowPrivilegeEscalation: false (no setuid gain), readOnlyRootFilesystem: true (immutable fs — needs emptyDir for writable paths), capabilities: drop: [ALL] then add only needed (e.g., NET_BIND_SERVICE), seccompProfile: RuntimeDefault. Set at Pod level (applies to all containers) with per-container overrides. This is the 'restricted' PSS profile in spec form.
scenarios.hint: Which three fields control user, escalation, and filesystem writability?

lessons.title: Cluster Architecture — Core concepts
concepts: Component roles: the apiserver is the only component clients talk to; etcd is the consistent key-value store of record; the scheduler binds unscheduled Pods to nodes; the controller-manager runs controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node) that reconcile desired vs actual state. kubelet (node agent) and kube-proxy (service networking) run on every node including control-plane nodes.
etcd: modern etcd needs ETCDCTL_API=3, the TLS endpoint, and the cluster's client certificates (found in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/).
Backup & restore: 'snapshot save' is the online backup API; copying the data dir of a running etcd risks corruption, and there is no 'kubectl backup etcd'.

Version skew: the supported skew policy: kube-apiserver first, then controller-manager/scheduler, then kubelets. kubelet can be at most two minor versions older than the apiserver (n-2) and never newer; kubectl must be within one minor version of the apiserver. kubeadm enforces this via 'kubeadm upgrade plan'.

Node affinity splits hard vs soft: requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is mandatory (Pod stays pending without SSD nodes); preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution adds weighted scoring the scheduler tries to satisfy. nodeSelector only does hard equality matching.

Pod affinity: daemonSet's contract is 'one Pod per selected node': the controller adds Pods as nodes join and removes them as nodes leave — perfect for node-level agents (log shippers, monitoring, CNI).

lessons.title: Services & Networking — Core concepts
concepts: Service DNS: cluster DNS form: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Your laptop's DNS is irrelevant.
Cross-namespace requires at least 'api.backend' (resolvable via search) — the FQDN always works.

Ingress TLS: spec.tls[] maps hosts to a TLS Secret (type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt/tls.key). NetworkPolicy ingress.from combines podSelector (who) with namespaceSelector (where) — both in one peer entry means AND. policyTypes: Ingress activates ingress enforcement; the podSelector selects the DB Pods; ports restrict to 5432.
TLS termination: without the tls section you get HTTP only. cert-manager automates issuance/renewal via ACME.

Ingress rules: kube-proxy watches Services/Endpoints and programs the data path on every node: iptables mode installs NAT rules (simple, scales to ~thousands of services), IPVS mode uses Linux IPVS (better load-balancing algorithms, scales further).

lessons.title: Storage — Core concepts
concepts: Binding requires: sufficient capacity, compatible accessModes, matching storageClassName (or both empty), and selector/label match.
Access modes: RWO (one node RW), ROX (many nodes read-only), RWX (many nodes RW).

StorageClass: reclaim policy is per-PV (defaulting from the StorageClass): Retain keeps the underlying volume after PVC deletion (data safe, manual cleanup, PV goes Released and can't rebind without manual intervention); Delete removes the volume asset.

Default class: a PVC with no storageClassName binds only to PVs with no class — unless a default StorageClass exists, in which case it's applied automatically and dynamic provisioning kicks in. Dynamically provisioned volumes usually default Delete; statically created PVs default Retain.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting — Core concepts
concepts: CrashLoopBackOff = container exits, kubelet backs off restarts.
Debug: --previous for the dead container's logs; common causes — bad command/args, missing env/config, failing startupProbe/livenessProbe killing slow boots, immediate exit (no foreground process).

imagePullSecrets: kubelet needs registry credentials: 'kubectl create secret docker-registry regcred --docker-server=... --docker-username=... --docker-password=...', then imagePullSecrets: [{name: regcred}] in the Pod spec (or on the ServiceAccount for all its Pods).
Pending is the scheduler telling you exactly what's wrong — read the events. Fix the cause (free disk, restart runtime), the node returns Ready and Pods reschedule.
Scheduler events: describe the Pod — events name the exact failure. 'kubectl describe pod' Events show each failed scheduling predicate.

lessons.title: Kubernetes Administration — Core concepts
concepts: A Pod is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers sharing network and storage. Deployments manage ReplicaSets, which keep the declared number of pods running via the reconciliation loop.
Services give pods stable virtual IPs and DNS names. A Service only routes to pods whose labels match its selector — empty endpoints almost always means a selector or readiness mismatch.
ConfigMaps and Secrets inject configuration as env vars or files. Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted by default — restrict RBAC and enable encryption at rest.
RBAC is allow-by-default-deny: Roles/ClusterRoles grant verbs on resources, Bindings attach them to users, groups, or service accounts. A binding to a deleted Role silently grants nothing.
PersistentVolumes decouple storage from pod lifecycle. A StorageClass with NoProvisioner never creates volumes dynamically — without matching pre-created PVs, PVCs stay Pending forever.

example.code:
kubectl get pods -n prod
kubectl describe pod api-7d9f8 -n prod
kubectl logs api-7d9f8 -n prod --previous
kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n prod --as=system:serviceaccount:prod:ci
example.walkthrough: This is the core admin triage loop: list, describe (events and status), check logs including the previous crashed instance, and verify permissions. Most cluster problems yield to this sequence before deeper tools are needed.

pitfalls: Common trap: deleting a crashing pod to 'fix' it — the ReplicaSet recreates the same broken spec; fix the spec, not the pod.
Common trap: editing a Service's selector to match pods without checking — you can accidentally route production traffic to the wrong workload.
Common trap: assuming pods restart on ConfigMap change — they don't; you need a rollout restart or checksum annotation.
Common trap: granting cluster-admin to 'make CI work' instead of scoping a Role to the namespace and verbs needed.

simulations.brief: kubectl get pods shows a pod in CrashLoopBackOff with 12 restarts. The deployment was updated an hour ago.
simulations.debrief: CrashLoopBackOff after a deploy = the new image or config is broken. Check the rollout: describe the pod for the exit reason, read the logs for the crash, then roll back the deployment — the fastest path to healthy.

evidence: FATAL: missing required env var DB_HOST
steps.explain: Exit code 1 with a FATAL log about a missing env var — the new deployment dropped a required variable. The fix: restore the env var (or roll back), not restart the pod — restarts will keep crashing.
options: Delete the pod and let it recreate
Fix the deployment: restore the DB_HOST env var (or roll back to the previous revision)

simulations.brief: A pod needs to land only on nodes with SSD storage. Choose the scheduling mechanism.
simulations.debrief: nodeSelector matches simple labels; affinity handles complex rules; taints repel. For 'only SSD nodes', label the nodes and use nodeSelector (or nodeAffinity) — the declarative way to constrain placement.

choices.feedback: Correct: labels + selector is the standard constraint.
choices.label: Label SSD nodes and add a nodeSelector

choices.feedback: Taints repel pods — the opposite of attracting to SSD nodes (unless combined with tolerations).
choices.label: Taint the SSD nodes

simulations.brief: Put these troubleshooting steps in order.
simulations.debrief: Symptoms first (get), then detail (describe), then evidence (logs), then fix. Skipping to the fix without evidence is how you 'fix' the wrong thing.

items: kubectl get pods — observe the symptom
kubectl describe pod/<name> — read events and state
kubectl logs <pod> — gather evidence
Fix the root cause (config, image, resources)

simulations.brief: This deployment manifest is headed for production. Click the misconfigured lines (2 issues to find).
simulations.debrief: Two reliability mistakes: no liveness/readiness probes (Kubernetes cannot detect or route around a hung app), and missing resource limits. Probes + resources are the production baseline.

steps.config:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: myapp:1.4.2

issues.description: No readiness/liveness probes — a hung container stays in service and receives traffic.
issues.fix: Add readinessProbe and livenessProbe (e.g. httpGet on /health).

issues.description: No resource requests/limits declared on the container.
issues.fix: Add resources.requests/limits for CPU and memory.

simulations.title: Review the deployment

consoleSims.brief: A node is running hot in the dashboard. Open the node view, check its pressure conditions, and cordon it for maintenance.
consoleSims.debrief: Node pressure (DiskPressure, MemoryPressure) explains scheduling failures. Cordoning stops new pods from landing while you investigate — drain follows when you are ready to evict.

tasks.instruction: Open the Nodes view in the dashboard.
Open node-2's detail page and read its conditions.
Cordon node-2 to prevent new scheduling.

consoleSims.brief: The api service needs to change from ClusterIP to NodePort for a debugging session. Edit the service in the dashboard.
consoleSims.debrief: Service type changes the exposure: ClusterIP is internal-only, NodePort opens a port on every node. Dashboards edit the same service object kubectl would — verify the type change took effect.

tasks.instruction: Open the api-svc service detail page.
Change the service type to NodePort.
Click Update to apply the change.

sections.heading: Cluster Architecture
items: Component roles — the apiserver is the only component clients talk to; etcd is the consistent key-value store of record; the scheduler binds unscheduled Pods to nodes; the controller-manager runs controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, Node) that reconcile desired vs actual sta…
Backup & restore — 'snapshot save' is the online backup API; copying the data dir of a running etcd risks corruption, and there is no 'kubectl backup etcd'.

Version skew — the supported skew policy: kube-apiserver first, then controller-manager/scheduler, then kubelets. kubelet can be at most two minor versions older than the apiserver (n-2) and never newer; kubectl must be within one minor version of the apiserver. kubeadm e…
Common trap — apiserver and etcd run on workers; scheduler and controller-manager run on control plane nodes only.
Common trap — apiserver: stores state; etcd: schedules Pods; scheduler: exposes the API; controller-manager: runs containers.
Common trap — version skew doesn't matter as long as kubectl matches the server.
Common trap — kubectl backup etcd --all-namespaces -o /backup/etcd.db.

sections.heading: Workloads & Scheduling
items: Taints repel Pods that don't tolerate them — 'kubectl taint nodes gpu1 dedicated=gpu:NoSchedule'.

Node affinity splits hard vs soft — requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution is mandatory (Pod stays pending without SSD nodes); preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution adds weighted scoring the scheduler tries to satisfy. nodeSelector only does hard equality matching.

Pod affinity — daemonSet's contract is 'one Pod per selected node': the controller adds Pods as nodes join and removes them as nodes leave — perfect for node-level agents (log shippers, monitoring, CNI).
Common trap — a static Pod copied to every node manually.
Common trap — taint the GPU nodes and add the toleration to every Pod so nothing breaks.
Common trap — kubectl taint worker-3 maintenance=true:NoSchedule.
Common trap — a Job with parallelism equal to node count.

sections.heading: Services & Networking
items: Service DNS — cluster DNS form: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Your laptop's DNS is irrelevant.
Cross-namespace — requires at least 'api.backend' (resolvable via search) — the FQDN always works.

Ingress TLS — spec.tls[] maps hosts to a TLS Secret (type kubernetes.io/tls with tls.crt/tls.key). NetworkPolicy ingress.from combines podSelector (who) with namespaceSelector (where) — both in one peer entry means AND. policyTypes: Ingress activates ingress enforcement;…
TLS termination — without the tls section you get HTTP only. cert-manager automates issuance/renewal via ACME.

Ingress rules — kube-proxy watches Services/Endpoints and programs the data path on every node: iptables mode installs NAT rules (simple, scales to ~thousands of services), IPVS mode uses Linux IPVS (better load-balancing algorithms, scales further).
Common trap — networkPolicies can't express cross-namespace rules.
Common trap — kube-proxy is a userspace proxy that terminates every connection.
Common trap — add the certificate as an annotation string on the Service.
Common trap — a Service of type LoadBalancer with a firewall annotation.

sections.heading: Storage
items: Binding requires — sufficient capacity, compatible accessModes, matching storageClassName (or both empty), and selector/label match.
Access modes — RWO (one node RW), ROX (many nodes read-only), RWX (many nodes RW).

StorageClass — reclaim policy is per-PV (defaulting from the StorageClass): Retain keeps the underlying volume after PVC deletion (data safe, manual cleanup, PV goes Released and can't rebind without manual intervention); Delete removes the volume asset.

Default class — a PVC with no storageClassName binds only to PVs with no class — unless a default StorageClass exists, in which case it's applied automatically and dynamic provisioning kicks in. Dynamically provisioned volumes usually default Delete; statically created PVs…
Common trap — dynamic provisioning works without any StorageClass.
Common trap — delete the PVC and recreate it bigger.
Common trap — RWO means one Pod total.
Common trap — pVCs bind to any PV regardless of size.

sections.heading: Troubleshooting
items: CrashLoopBackOff — CrashLoopBackOff = container exits, kubelet backs off restarts.
Debug — --previous for the dead container's logs; common causes — bad command/args, missing env/config, failing startupProbe/livenessProbe killing slow boots, immediate exit (no foreground process).
Pending is the scheduler telling you exactly what's wrong — read the events. Fix the cause (free disk, restart runtime), the node returns Ready and Pods reschedule.
Scheduler events — describe the Pod — events name the exact failure. 'kubectl describe pod' Events show each failed scheduling predicate.
Common trap — static Pods self-heal without etcd.
Common trap — pull the image manually on each node with docker pull.
Common trap — imagePullBackOff means the tag is wrong.
Common trap — pending means the image is pulling.

sections.heading: Security
items: RBAC — 'kubectl auth can-i <verb> <resource> --as=<user> -n <ns>' evaluates RBAC as that subject — the definitive 'can they?' check.

ServiceAccounts — hardening: per-workload ServiceAccounts (never share default), least-privilege Roles/RoleBindings, automountServiceAccountToken: false on Pods that don't call the API, and short-lived projected tokens (the default since 1.22 — auto-rotating, audience-bound).

Pod Security Standards — set at Pod level (applies to all containers) with per-container overrides.
Common trap — RBAC can enforce Pod security fields directly.
Common trap — audit logs don't exist in Kubernetes.
Common trap — encrypt each Secret's values manually before creating.
Common trap — run as root but add a NetworkPolicy.

checklist: Get 7–8 hours of sleep the night before — fatigue destroys recall faster than any topic gap.
Bring valid government-issued photo ID and arrive at the test center 30 minutes early.
Eat a real meal beforehand; bring water and a light snack if the center allows them.
Read every question twice before scanning the answer choices.
Flag uncertain questions and move on — return with fresh eyes at the end.
Eliminate the obviously wrong answers first, then compare the survivors.
Budget your time: answer steadily and keep a 10–15 minute review buffer.
Re-run your weakest-domain drill until mastery is at least 80%.
